The catalog records what is open. This is the attempt to close some of it: one study a
week, each aimed at a single entry, taken in priority order.

Scope is target trial emulation only: the specification of an emulated protocol, the
g-methods used to estimate the effects of sustained treatment strategies, and the
benchmarking of emulations against the trials they emulate. A problem that would be the
same problem in any observational analysis is out of scope, because it is not what this
catalog is about.



## Completed

### [BEN-02](problems/BEN-02-replication-is-reported-as-a-binary-label-rather-than-as-a-c.qmd): A binary replication label changes with precision alone, and one operator carries almost all of it

**Question.** BEN-02 says replication is reported as a binary label that mixes estimand mismatch with random error. Holding the true trial-emulation discrepancy fixed, how much of the label is decided by precision rather than by the discrepancy, and which of the operators in use carries that sensitivity?

**Answer.** For the operators tested, yes, and it is concentrated in one of them. The sensitivity S is the larger of the two operator-specific values at 0.4915, against a threshold of 0.10 declared before the run, with a 95 percent Monte Carlo interval of 0.4903 to 0.4931; the lower endpoint clears the threshold by roughly 538 Monte Carlo standard errors. Confidence-interval overlap supplies that value; direction agreement moves by 0.1244 over the same range. Two benchmark pairs carrying the same true discrepancy can therefore be labeled agreeing and disagreeing on the strength of how precisely each was estimated, and the operator most used to produce the label is the most exposed.

**What it does not answer.** S is the maximum over the operators tested, so the result is an at-least-one-operator claim: it establishes that interval overlap is materially precision-sensitive and that direction agreement is less so, not that every binary replication label is. It holds for these two illustrative operators, these 16 fixed scenarios and these three nested precision levels. This is the pair-level component of BEN-02 and not the entry as a whole: it says nothing about between-pair heterogeneity across a benchmarking program, about calibration of a graded metric against a decision, or about the graded alternatives the entry's own audit established already exist, all three of which the design review named as out of scope and which are declared limitations rather than results. Outcomes are binary at a single horizon, so the behavior of these operators on a time-to-event scale is untouched.

### [CNF-01](problems/CNF-01-convergence-of-treatment-in-the-comparator-arm-attenuates-th.qmd): A single cumulative-initiation number at the horizon does not determine the attenuation it is asked to explain

**Question.** CNF-01 asks authors to publish the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms so a reader can see how far the contrasted strategies stayed distinct, and to quantify by simulation how much attenuation a given convergence rate produces. Does that diagnostic actually recover the attenuation?

**Answer.** No. Within the simulated grid, comparator-arm cumulative initiation at 120 months does not uniquely determine attenuation: matched early and late initiation scenarios, whose reported diagnostic agrees to within 0.0005, differ in attenuation by 0.0528 to 0.2027. Nine of the twelve matched pairs exceed the 0.05 threshold declared before the run by at least three Monte Carlo standard errors, at 5 to 46 of them; the other three sit within 3 and are individually inconclusive, and all three are at the lowest convergence rate, where there is least attenuation to misattribute. A single cumulative-incidence value at the horizon is therefore insufficient for recovering attenuation in these scenarios. What the reported number cannot see is when the comparator arm initiated and who initiated.

**What it does not answer.** The comparison holds the diagnostic fixed only at 120 months. At earlier horizons the early and late scenarios differ in observed cumulative initiation by as much as 0.269, so those contrasts are not comparisons at equal C(h) and cannot independently establish insufficiency there. The study establishes that C(120) alone is insufficient within this grid. It does not establish that reporting C is necessary, that the full initiation curve would be sufficient, or that a universal conversion from convergence to attenuation exists. The comparator arm converges upward and the treated arm never discontinues, so this is one direction of convergence only. There is no loss to follow-up and no competing event, both excluded so the attenuation is not confounded with a second mechanism. The scale is the risk difference throughout; a hazard ratio would mix this mechanism with non-collapsibility.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CNF-01-convergence-attenuation/out/CNF-01.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CNF-01-convergence-attenuation/out/CNF-01.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CNF-01-convergence-attenuation/out/CNF-01.odt)

### [PRO-02](problems/PRO-02-inference-conditions-on-a-fixed-target-trial-that-was-in-fac.qmd): A recorded, effect-blind search over highly correlated protocols leaves naive intervals close to nominal on average, and undercovering when the candidates disagree

**Question.** PRO-02 says inference conditions on a fixed target trial that was in fact selected after seeing the data. When the search is recorded and the selector is blind to the treatment effect, choosing among 4 or 16 candidate protocols by outcome counts or covariate-outcome associations, how much coverage do naive 95% intervals for the selected protocol lose, and what do Bonferroni correction and sample splitting cost?

**Answer.** Not materially, within this design. The global deficit D_all was 0.0015 (simultaneous 95% Monte Carlo interval -0.0001 to 0.0030) and D_nonboundary 0.0023 (0.0004 to 0.0042), both upper limits far below the registered 0.02 threshold; all 360 fixed-candidate evaluations passed the calibration gate. The nonboundary deficit is detectably above zero, but it is about a fifth of a percentage point. Averaged over replicates, a recorded, effect-blind choice among these protocols costs naive intervals almost nothing.

**What it does not answer.** The conclusion covers deterministic recorded searches over nested age thresholds and outcome horizons, libraries of 4 or 16 highly correlated candidates, treatment-effect-blind selectors, and correctly specified inverse probability weighting. It does not cover undocumented or sequential protocol development by an analyst who has seen results, other protocol components such as grace periods or treatment definitions, libraries of weakly correlated protocols, or misspecified weights. The replication's calibration gate controls false failure across 360 comparisons and in exchange would pass a candidate miscalibrated by less than about two percentage points.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/PRO-02-ben-02-recorded-protocol-search/out/PRO-02.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/PRO-02-ben-02-recorded-protocol-search/out/PRO-02.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/PRO-02-ben-02-recorded-protocol-search/out/PRO-02.odt)

### [ELG-01](problems/ELG-01-an-unrecorded-eligibility-criterion-is-indistinguishable-fro.qmd): Unrecorded eligibility changes who is eligible more than it changes the effect among them

**Question.** ELG-01 says that when the measurement defining eligibility is missing for some patients, the eligible population is not identified without validation data. When two data-generating laws produce identical records but differ in eligibility among the unrecorded, can they imply materially different 60-month risk differences among the truly eligible? And how do estimators with and without an internal validation sample perform?

**Answer.** Not materially different, within this design. The registered structural contrast Delta_ID was -0.00066 (90% interval -0.000661 to -0.000660), inside the equivalence band of plus or minus 0.005, and the observed records and every no-validation method output were identical across the pair as required. Latent eligibility changed who was eligible, not the effect among them: the same shift raised the true prevalence of eligibility from 0.705 to 0.787, which estimators assuming eligibility is missing at random missed by up to 0.082, while every estimator's risk difference was unbiased within plus or minus 0.005 in all 48 scenarios.

**What it does not answer.** The result is conditional on one baseline threshold criterion, a binary 60-month outcome, correctly specified models and a single effect modifier whose link to hidden eligibility is moderate. It cannot estimate a real-world shift or establish empirical materiality, and a hidden eligibility mechanism tied more strongly to the effect modifier could change the effect materially. It does not cover external, nonprobability or unknown-probability validation, validation measured with error, time-varying eligibility, treatment switching, censoring or unmeasured treatment confounding.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/ELG-01-latent-eligibility-validation/out/ELG-01.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/ELG-01-latent-eligibility-validation/out/ELG-01.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/ELG-01-latent-eligibility-validation/out/ELG-01.odt)

### [ELG-02](problems/ELG-02-eligibility-criteria-built-from-healthcare-use-variables-can.qmd): Restriction on a healthcare-use collider biases an emulation materially, and a measured-variable screen adds nothing that adjusting for the measured variables does not

**Question.** ELG-02 says eligibility criteria built from prior healthcare use are applied without checking whether they are colliders. Under known graphs, how much bias does restriction on such a criterion produce, how much of the restricted-versus-broad contrast is a legitimate change of target, and does screening an external sample for a collider signal and responding to the result estimate the restricted effect better than analyses that do not screen?

**Answer.** Materially consequential, within this benchmark. The minimal restricted estimator's absolute bias reached 0.036 with coverage 0.728 when the criterion was a strong collider, and five of the twelve collider cells had a lower 95% Monte Carlo bound of at least the registered 0.010, spanning both orientations, both retention levels and two edge strengths. The two-strength condition rests on one cell at strength 0.45 whose lower bound is 0.0112; without it the classification would be mixed. The screen-and-respond policy is conditionally beneficial by the registered rule when the collider parents are measured (7 of 12 collider cells) and not beneficial when they are not, but the benefit is not the screen's: adjusting for every measured variable without screening does as well, and pooling the audit sample into the analysis does better in every cell.

**What it does not answer.** The study is a mechanism benchmark under correctly specified probit models and a known four-node graph. It does not discover or certify collider status for an unknown eligibility criterion, identify an unnamed latent cause, or estimate how often real criteria are colliders. The screen's operating characteristics do not transfer to indirect paths, association-mimicking noncolliders, nonlinear mechanisms, noisy proxies, partial measurement or audit samples of other sizes, and the two analyst views are the extremes of every parent measured perfectly and neither measured at all.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/ELG-02-baseline-healthcare-use-selection/out/ELG-02.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/ELG-02-baseline-healthcare-use-selection/out/ELG-02.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/ELG-02-baseline-healthcare-use-selection/out/ELG-02.odt)

## How a problem gets chosen

Not every open problem can be settled by a study, and the difference is not cosmetic.
A simulation can measure bias, coverage and error rates, and it can show how badly a
known nonidentification bites at realistic sample sizes. It cannot establish that a
package is missing, that clinicians misread a plot, that a field under-reports
something, or that a quantity is unidentifiable in principle. Those need software, a
case study, a meta-research corpus, or a proof.

Every one of the 43 catalog entries was judged on both questions separately,
by an external model, before the program started: is this a target trial emulation
problem, and what kind of study would settle it. The queue below is the intersection.

::: {.table-scroll}

| Why an entry is not in the program | n |
|---|---:|
| needs analytic, not a simulation or case study | 9 |
| not a target trial emulation problem | 8 |
| needs corpus, not a simulation or case study | 5 |
| needs consensus, not a simulation or case study | 3 |
| needs software, not a simulation or case study | 1 |

:::

## What each study has to do

Simulation studies follow ADEMP: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods,
performance measures ([Morris, White and Crowther 2019](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086)).
Two rules follow from it and are enforced rather than encouraged.

Every performance measure carries a Monte Carlo standard error.
:   A bias of 0.02 is uninterpretable without knowing whether the Monte Carlo error is
    0.001 or 0.03. The replicate count is derived in the protocol from a target Monte
    Carlo standard error, not chosen because it is a round number.

Failed replicates are results.
:   A method that converges on 60% of replicates and is unbiased on those is not an
    unbiased method. Convergence is reported for every method in every scenario.

The protocol is committed before the run.
:   It fixes the design and states in advance what result would count as showing the
    problem is real and what would count as showing it is not. The commit that adds it
    is the timestamp.

Code, protocols and results are at
[github.com/choxos/TTE-open-problems/tree/main/studies](https://github.com/choxos/TTE-open-problems/tree/main/studies).
